chunks: When a motor or solenoid draws most current. The question: When does a motor/solenoid draw the most current?
A DC motor draws the most current when it is not turning: at the moment it starts, or when its shaft is jammed.
A spinning motor makes its own voltage that opposes the supply, called back-EMF. At zero speed there is no back-EMF, so only the winding's small resistance limits the current.
A DC solenoid is simpler: it draws its largest current at steady state, once it has settled.
Think of starting a loaded bicycle from a standstill. The first push takes the most effort. Once you are rolling, the bike helps carry you, and the effort drops.
A motor behaves the same way. Starting and getting up to speed takes a big gulp of current. A jammed shaft is like holding the bike still against the pedals: it keeps gulping.
At t = 0 the rotor is stationary so E equals 0 and the only things between the supply and the loop are R and L.
The current then climbs with tau e equals L over R while E rises with speed and chokes it off.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed, opposing the supply. Stall current: the current when the shaft cannot turn, equal to V over R .
Winding resistance: the small resistance of the motor's coil. Time constant ( L over R ): how fast current builds up in a coil ("Inductor at t = 0⁺ and DC steady state").
Inrush current: the large current right after switching on.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor with 1 ohms of winding resistance. At rest, there is no back-EMF, so the current is 12 over 1 equals 12 amps.
When the motor is spinning freely at nearly full speed, the back-EMF might be 11. 5 volts. The current is then (12 minus 11. 5) over 1 equals 0. 5 amps.
The inductance delays the rise by a few milliseconds, so the actual peak is a bit under 12 amps. That is the whole idea.

"A motor draws the most current when it's stalled or just starting, because there's no back-EMF to oppose the supply: I equals V minus K e omega over R, so at zero speed it's V over R, say 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm, versus half an amp at free-running speed.
Inductance only delays it by a few milliseconds. The same goes for a jammed or heavily loaded motor.
A DC solenoid draws its maximum, V over R, at steady state once the plunger is seated."
